retrieved_papers.abstract: We propose Prototypical Networks for the problem of few-shot classification, where a classifier must generalize to new classes not seen in the training set, given only a small number of examples of each new class. Prototypical Networks learn a metric space in which classification can be performed by computing distances to prototype representations of each class. Compared to recent approaches for few-shot learning, they reflect a simpler inductive bias that is beneficial in this limited-data regime, and achieve excellent results. We provide an analysis showing that some simple design decisions can yield substantial improvements over recent approaches involving complicated architectural choices and meta-learning. We further extend Prototypical Networks to zero-shot learning and achieve state-of-the-art results on the CU-Birds dataset.

retrieved_papers.abstract: Attributed networks nowadays are ubiquitous in a myriad of high-impact applications, such as social network analysis, financial fraud detection, and drug discovery. As a central analytical task on attributed networks, node classification has received much attention in the research community. In real-world attributed networks, a large portion of node classes only contains limited labeled instances, rendering a long-tail node class distribution. Existing node classification algorithms are unequipped to handle the few-shot node classes. As a remedy, few-shot learning has attracted a surge of attention in the research community. Yet, few-shot node classification remains a challenging problem as we need to address the following questions: (i) How to extract meta-knowledge from an attributed network for few-shot node classification? (ii) How to identify the informativeness of each labeled instance for building a robust and effective model? To answer these questions, in this paper, we propose a graph meta-learning framework -- Graph Prototypical Networks (GPN). By constructing a pool of semi-supervised node classification tasks to mimic the real test environment, GPN is able to perform meta-learning on an attributed network and derive a highly generalizable model for handling the target classification task. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superior capability of GPN in few-shot node classification.

retrieved_papers.abstract: Abstract Few-Shot Learning (FSL) aims at recognizing the target classes that only a few samples are available for training. The current approaches mostly address FSL by learning a generalized class-level metric while neglect the intra-class distribution information. In this work, we propose Improved Prototypical Networks (IPN) to address this issue. Inspired by the observation that the intra-class samples differ greatly in revealing the class distribution, we first propose an attention-analogous strategy to explore the class distribution information by distributing different weights to samples based on their representativeness. Besides, to further explore the discriminative information across classes, we propose a distance scaling strategy to reduce the intra-class difference while enlarge the inter-class difference. The experimental results on two benchmark datasets show the superiority of the proposed model against the state-of-the-art approaches.

retrieved_papers.abstract: Although providing exceptional results for many computer vision tasks, state-of-the-art deep learning algorithms catastrophically struggle in low data scenarios. However, if data in additional modalities exist (e.g. text) this can compensate for the lack of data and improve the classification results. To overcome this data scarcity, we design a cross-modal feature generation framework capable of enriching the low populated embedding space in few-shot scenarios, leveraging data from the auxiliary modality. Specifically, we train a generative model that maps text data into the visual feature space to obtain more reliable prototypes. This allows to exploit data from additional modalities (e.g. text) during training while the ultimate task at test time remains classification with exclusively visual data. We show that in such cases nearest neighbor classification is a viable approach and outperform state-of-the-art single-modal and multimodal few-shot learning methods on the CUB-200 and Oxford-102 datasets.

retrieved_papers.title: Gaussian Prototypical Networks for Few-Shot Learning on Omniglot

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.02735, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

retrieved_papers.abstract: We propose a novel architecture for k-shot classification on the Omniglot dataset. Building on prototypical networks, we extend their architecture to what we call Gaussian prototypical networks. Prototypical networks learn a map between images and embedding vectors, and use their clustering for classification. In our model, a part of the encoder output is interpreted as a confidence region estimate about the embedding point, and expressed as a Gaussian covariance matrix. Our network then constructs a direction and class dependent distance metric on the embedding space, using uncertainties of individual data points as weights. We show that Gaussian prototypical networks are a preferred architecture over vanilla prototypical networks with an equivalent number of parameters. We report results consistent with state-of-the-art performance in 1-shot and 5-shot classification both in 5-way and 20-way regime on the Omniglot dataset. We explore artificially down-sampling a fraction of images in the training set, which improves our performance. Our experiments therefore lead us to hypothesize that Gaussian prototypical networks might perform better in less homogeneous, noisier datasets, which are commonplace in real world applications.

retrieved_papers.abstract: Existing few-shot learning models leverage vision-language pre-trained models to alleviate the data scarcity problem. However, such models usually process visual and text information separately, which causes still inherent disparities between cross-modal features. Therefore, we propose the ProFusion model, which leverages multimodal pre-trained models and prototypical networks to construct multiple prototypes. Specifically, ProFusion generates image and text prototypes symmetrically using the visual encoder and text encoder, while integrating visual and text information through the fusion module to create more expressive multimodal feature fusion prototypes. Additionally, we introduce the alignment module to ensure consistency between image and text prototypes. During inference, ProFusion calculates the similarity of test images to the three types of prototypes separately and applies a weighted sum to generate the final prediction. Experiments demonstrate that ProFusion performs outstanding classification tasks on 15 benchmark datasets.

retrieved_papers.abstract: Prototypical network (PN) is a simple yet effective few shot learning strategy. It is a metric-based meta-learning technique where classification is performed by computing Euclidean distances to prototypical representations of each class. Conventional PN attributes equal importance to all samples and generates prototypes by simply averaging the support sample embeddings belonging to each class. In this work, we propose a novel version of PN that attributes weights to support samples corresponding to their influence on the support sample distribution. Influence weights of samples are calculated based on maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) between the mean embeddings of sample distributions including and excluding the sample. Comprehensive evaluation of our proposed influential PN (IPNet) is performed by comparing its performance with other baseline PNs on three different benchmark dermatological datasets. IPNet outperforms all baseline models with compelling results across all three datasets and various N -way, K-shot classification tasks. Findings from cross-domain adaptation experiments further establish the generalizability of IPNet.

Jake Snell $^{1*}$ , Kevin Swersky $^{2}$  & Richard S. Zemel $^{1}$

ABSTRACT

A recent approach to few-shot classification called matching networks has demonstrated the benefits of coupling metric learning with a training procedure that mimics test. This approach relies on an attention scheme that forms a distribution over all points in the support set, scaling poorly with its size. We propose a more streamlined approach, prototypical networks, that learns a metric space in which few-shot classification can be performed by computing Euclidean distances to prototype repres
1 INTRODUCTION

One-shot classification (Miller et al., 2000; Lake et al., 2011; Koch, 2015) (and more generally, few-shot classification) is a problem in which a classifier must be adapted to accommodate new classes not seen in training, given only a single  $(n)$  example(s) of these classes. A classical approach, such as retraining the model on the new data, would severely overfit. While the problem is quite difficult, it has been demonstrated that people have the ability to successfully perform one-shot cla

To overcome this, much progress has been made recently in applying metric learning (Goldberger et al., 2004; Kulis, 2012; Bellet et al., 2013) to one-shot tasks. Most recently, (Vinyals et al., 2016) proposed a metric learning approach that they call matching networks. This approach uses an attention mechanism over a learned embedding of the support set in order to predict class labels for the points to be classified, a.k.a the "query set". It optionally allows the embeddings to be conditioned o

In this paper, we propose a few-shot learning classifier based on a relatively simple idea: there exists an embedding, where points belonging to a class cluster around a single prototype. This inductive bias is a useful one to combat overfitting for one-shot tasks. Our approach also comes with the benefit that it is very simple to implement, and computationally fast. In order to do this, we learn a non-linear mapping of the input into an embedding space using a neural network, and take the class

prototype to be the mean of the support set in the embedding space. Classification is then performed by simply finding the nearest prototype to the embedded query point. We find that this approach yields competitive results with matching networks and other one-shot learning approaches, despite being much simpler.

A related problem is known as zero-shot learning, where instead of being given a small number of examples of a new class at test-time, each class comes with a set of meta-information, often attributes, that give a high level description of that class. The idea then is to learn a mapping from input examples to the high-level attributes of their member class. We adapt the idea of prototypical networks to this setting by learning a secondary embedding of the attribute vector such that the image emb
2 RELATED WORK

Neighborhood Components Analysis (NCA) (Goldberger et al., 2004) learns a Mahalanobis distance to maximize K-nearest-neighbour's (KNN) leave-one-out accuracy in the transformed space. A distribution over the neighbors of each data point is computed according to a softmax over the corresponding Mahalanobis distances. This distribution is marginalized to form a distribution over class assignments and the projection matrix is updated via gradient descent to maximize the probability of the true clas

Our approach is similar to the nearest class mean approach of (Mensink et al., 2013) from the metric learning literature, where each class is represented by the mean of its examples, and classification is performed by finding the prototype that is closest to the query point. Their approach was developed to rapidly incorporate new classes into a classifier without retraining, however it relies on a linear embedding and is designed to handle the case where the novel classes come with many examples

In matching networks (Vinyals et al., 2016) they propose a meta-learning strategy in which training mimics test by stochastically creating one-shot "episodes". We adopt the same strategy when training our models. They, like us, use neural networks to non-linearly transform data points into a space that is more amenable to classification. However, matching networks make predictions by computing attention weights over each point in the support set. This becomes computationally expensive as the siz

The neural statistician (Edwards & Storkey, 2016) extends the variational autoencoder (Kingma & Welling, 2013) to learn generative models of datasets rather than individual points. One component of the neural statistician is the "statistic network" which summarizes a set of data points into a statistic vector. It does this by encoding each point within a dataset, taking a sample mean, and applying a post-processing network to obtain an approximate posterior over the statistic vector. Edwards & S

is a discriminative model which is more appropriate because our primary task, one-shot learning, is also discriminative. Discriminative training has the added benefit of lending our model more flexibility in both the way we compute summary statistics and use them to make predictions at test time.

There are many other approaches to one-shot learning that employ very different techniques from ours. Koch uses siamese networks to predict the probability that two images belong to the same class. Lake et al. devise a hierarchical Bayesian generative model of how a handwritten character is created in order to perform one-shot learning on the Omniglot dataset. Santoro et al. propose memory augmented neural networks (MANN) that reference an external memory in a similar fashion to neural Turing ma
3 PROTOTYPICAL NETWORKS

At prediction time we are given a support set of  $N$  labeled examples:  $S = \{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i = 1}^{N} = S^{1}\cup \ldots \cup$ $S^K$  where  $S^k = \{(x,y)\in S\mid y = k\}$ . Our method computes a class representation  $c_{k}$ , or prototype, of each class through an embedding function  $f_{\theta}(x)$  parameterized by learnable parameters  $\theta$ :
Given a test point  $\tilde{x}$ , prototypical networks form a distribution over classes based on a softmax over the Euclidean distances between its embedding and the prototypes:
Learning proceeds by maximizing the log-probability of the true class  $\tilde{y}$ :

We train in an episodic manner similar to Vinyals et al. (2016) by randomly selecting a subset of classes from the training set, then choosing a subset of examples within each class to act as the support set and the remainder to serve as test points.
3.1 PROTOTYPE NORMALIZATION

In episodic training, the support set is randomly chosen from among the training points. In datasets with high variability this can lead to a large variance in the class prototypes,  $c$ , between episodes. In order to reduce this variability, we found that it can sometimes be beneficial to normalize the prototypes,  $\bar{c}_k = \frac{c_k}{\|c_k\|}$  and use  $\bar{c}_k$  in place of  $c_k$  in Equation (2). 3.2 PREDICTING THE WEIGHTS OF A LINEAR CLASSIFIER

A simple analysis is useful in gaining insight into the nature of the learned classifier (a similar analysis appears in Mensink et al. (2013)). When we use Euclidean distance to measure the distance between a query point and the class prototypes, then the loss function in (2) is equivalent to a linear classifier with a particular parameterization. To see this, we expand the term within the exponent:
The first term in Equation (4) is constant with respect to the class  $k$ , so it does not affect the softmax probabilities. We can write the remaining terms as a linear classifier as follows:

We can view this through the lens of meta-learning, where the model is predicting the weights and biases of a linear classifier using a simple function of the mean of the embedded support set. By contrast, the predictive function in matching networks is a generalization of a nearest neighbor classifier, rather than a linear classifier.

When using prototype normalization, the biases  $b_{k}$  will all be 1, and the class weights  $w_{k}$  will be restricted to have a norm of 2. In this case, using Euclidean distance becomes proportional to cosine distance.

A natural question is whether it makes sense to use multiple prototypes per class instead of just one. If each support point were to be considered a prototype, then this would be analogous to doing nearest neighbor classification in the embedding space, which would be computationally expensive. 3.3 DESIGN CHOICES

There are still a number of design choices that need to be made with this model in order to achieve optimal performance. One such choice is in deciding how many classes we would like the classifier to operate over during each training episode. For example, at test time we might be evaluating on 5-way classification, but at training time we could train each episode with 20-way classification. We found in general that training on a larger number of classes per episode improves performance, even if

Another choice involves the possible decoupling of the  $n$  in  $n$ -shot between training and testing. We could train on 1-shot, but test on 5-shot or vice-versa. We found that it is typically better to match the shot at training and testing; that is, when it comes to the shot, to match the training procedure to the test procedure. We demonstrate this empirically in the Experiments section below.
Finally, we need to specify whether to use prototype normalization. We found that normalization generally acts as a regularizer and speeds up training.
4 EXPERIMENTS

For few-shot learning, we performed experiments on Omniglot (Lake et al., 2011), the miniImagenet version of ILSVRC-2012 (Russakovsky et al., 2015) proposed by (Vinyals et al., 2016). For zero-shot learning, we perform experiments on the 2011 version of the Caltech UCSD bird dataset (CUB200 2011) (Welinder et al., 2010).
4.1 OMNIGLOT

Omniglot (Lake et al., 2011) is a dataset of 1623 handwritten characters collected from 50 alphabets. There are 20 examples associated with each character, where each example was drawn by a different human subject. We follow the procedure of (Vinyals et al., 2016) by augmenting the characters with rotations in multiples of 90 degrees and using 1200 characters for training and the remainder for evaluation. We trained prototypical networks using episodes designed for 1-shot learning, i.e., the support sets during training consist of a single input example, and we train using 20-way classification. Our results are as good or better than those reported in matching networks, and to our knowledge represent the state-of-the-art on this dataset using these splits.
4.2 miniIMAGENET

The miniImageNet dataset (Vinyals et al., 2016) is derived from the larger ImageNet dataset (Deng et al., 2009). It consists of 60,000 color images of size  $84 \times 84$  divided into 100 classes with 600 examples each. It is designed for testing one-shot learning algorithms, where 80 classes are chosen for training, and 20 for testing.

5 CONCLUSION

We have proposed a simple method called prototypical networks for few-shot learning based on the idea that we can represent each class by the mean of its examples in a representation space learned by a neural network. We train these networks to specifically perform well in the few-shot setting by using episodic training. Prototypical networks are simple to implement, and computationally efficient. - ORIG-EXP: strength: The experiments show the method’s generality across Omniglot, miniImageNet, and zero-shot CUB, including evaluation of train/test shot matching and 20-way episode design choices. weakness: The datasets and protocols are mostly inherited from prior work, so the experimental originality is modest; the paper does not introduce a new benchmark or substantially new evaluation protocol. evidence: SRC-038(page=3), SRC-040(page=4), SRC-041(page=4), SRC-043(page=4), SRC-044(page=4), SRC-047(page=4), SRC-050(page=5).
- ORIG-COM: strength: The paper creatively combines nearest-class-mean representations, learned nonlinear metric embeddings, and episodic meta-learning into a method that is simpler and more scalable than attention over support examples. The rationale for the combination is clear: a single class prototype is an inductive bias against overfitting and reduces support-set scaling costs. weakness: Since each component has clear antecedents, the originality depends on the strength of the integration; some readers may view it as a natural extension of nearest class mean plus matching-network-style training. evidence: SRC-010(page=0), SRC-015(page=1), SRC-016(page=1), SRC-018(page=2), SRC-024(page=2).
- ORIG-NEG: strength: The paper gives useful critical comparisons, especially that matching networks scale poorly because they attend over all support examples, and discusses why multiple prototypes or support-point-as-prototype variants may be computationally or procedurally less attractive. weakness: These are not rigorous negative results or systematic failure analyses; they are primarily motivation and design rationale rather than controlled critical assessments. evidence: SRC-006(page=0), SRC-009(page=0), SRC-016(page=1), SRC-032(page=3).

Evidence anchors used:
- SRC-006(page=0): Supports the originality claim that the proposed method avoids matching networks’ support-set attention and aims to improve simplicity and scalability.
- SRC-008(page=0): Establishes that one-shot/few-shot classification is an existing problem rather than a newly introduced task.
- SRC-010(page=0): Supports the central methodological contribution: learning an embedding where each class clusters around a single prototype.
- SRC-011(page=1): Supports the prototype-as-mean and nearest-prototype classification mechanism.
- SRC-012(page=1): Supports the zero-shot extension using attribute embeddings as class prototypes.
- SRC-014(page=1): Shows relationship to NCA and clarifies how the paper distinguishes its class-level softmax from point-level metric learning.
- SRC-015(page=1): Shows closeness to nearest class mean methods and the claimed distinction via nonlinear embedding and few-shot episodic training.
- SRC-016(page=1): Supports the creative combination with episodic training and the contrast against matching networks’ attention over support examples.
- SRC-018(page=2): Supports the argument that the model is a discriminative set-summary method, distinguishing it from neural statistician.
- SRC-021(page=2): Provides the formal prototype computation setup.
- SRC-022(page=2): Provides the formal distance-based class probability mechanism.
- SRC-024(page=2): Supports the use of episodic training adopted from Vinyals et al.
- SRC-026(page=2): Supports prototype normalization as a design refinement rather than the main novelty.
- SRC-028(page=2): Supports the analysis connecting Euclidean prototype classification to a linear classifier and notes similarity to prior work.
- SRC-030(page=3): Supports the meta-learning interpretation as predicting linear classifier weights and biases from support-set means.
- SRC-032(page=3): Supports discussion of single versus multiple prototypes and tradeoffs against nearest-neighbor or partitioning approaches.
- SRC-034(page=3): Supports originality in practical design insight about training with more classes per episode.
- SRC-035(page=3): Supports the design insight about matching training and test shot.
- SRC-038(page=3): Supports that experiments use existing few-shot and zero-shot datasets.
- SRC-040(page=4): Supports that the Omniglot setup follows a prior protocol and architecture style.
- SRC-041(page=4): Supports empirical evidence of competitive/state-of-the-art performance on Omniglot.
- SRC-043(page=4): Supports that miniImageNet is an existing benchmark designed for one-shot algorithms.
- SRC-044(page=4): Supports the experimental comparison of 1-shot versus 5-shot training and evaluation.
- SRC-047(page=4): Supports that the CUB zero-shot experiment uses an existing dataset and split.
- SRC-050(page=5): Supports the zero-shot implementation using AlexNet image embeddings and linear attribute-to-prototype mapping.
- SRC-051(page=5): Supports the claim of strong zero-shot empirical performance without structured SVMs.

Key questions for the authors:
- Can the authors more sharply characterize when the single-prototype-per-class assumption is expected to be valid, especially for multimodal classes?
- How much of the originality and performance comes from episodic training versus the class-mean prototype objective itself?
- Would a controlled comparison against nonlinear nearest class mean trained without episodic episodes better isolate the methodological novelty?
- Can the zero-shot attribute-prototype extension be framed more explicitly relative to prior label-embedding methods, since the conceptual overlap appears substantial?

Recommendation: Accept

Reviewer dimension: POL

Paper summary: The paper proposes prototypical networks for few-shot classification and extends the method to zero-shot learning using class attributes, with experiments on Omniglot, miniImageNet/ImageNet-derived data, and CUB-200 birds.

Dimension score (1-10): 4

Confidence (1-5): 4

Sub-dimension scores:
- POL-ETH: 4/10
- POL-DAT: 4/10
- POL-ANO: 1/10
- POL-PLG: 7/10
- POL-IMP: 3/10

Strengths:
- The work appears to use established benchmark datasets and cites their sources for Omniglot, miniImageNet/ImageNet, and CUB-200 rather than presenting undocumented private data (SRC-038(page=3), SRC-040(page=4), SRC-043(page=4), SRC-047(page=4)).
- The paper gives enough high-level dataset descriptions and split procedures to identify the data sources and experimental setting, including Omniglot subject-written characters, miniImageNet class counts, and CUB-200 images/attributes (SRC-040(page=4), SRC-043(page=4), SRC-047(page=4), SRC-050(page=5)).
- Related work is cited throughout, and the paper distinguishes its method from matching networks, nearest-class-mean methods, and neural statistician approaches (SRC-015(page=1), SRC-016(page=1), SRC-017(page=1)).
- The technical contribution appears low immediate-risk compared with generative, surveillance, or human-subject decision systems, since experiments are limited to image/character/bird classification benchmarks (SRC-038(page=3)).

Weaknesses:
- The submission is not anonymized: it includes author names, institutional affiliations, and acknowledgments, which would be a severe violation if the venue requires double-blind review (SRC-002(page=0), SRC-003(page=0), SRC-004(page=0), SRC-055(page=5), SRC-056(page=5)).
- There is no explicit ethics, broader-impact, or responsible-AI discussion, despite the method targeting rapid adaptation to new classes and being applicable beyond benign benchmarks (SRC-010(page=0), SRC-012(page=1), SRC-054(page=5)).
- The paper does not discuss dataset licenses, permitted uses, consent, privacy status, or restrictions for Omniglot, ImageNet/miniImageNet, or CUB-200, even though these datasets involve human-generated handwriting, web-scale images, and annotated image data (SRC-040(page=4), SRC-043(page=4), SRC-047(page=4), SRC-050(page=5)).
- There is no IRB/ethics approval statement or explanation of why one is unnecessary for the use of human-subject-derived Omniglot characters or potentially human-curated/annotated image datasets (SRC-040(page=4), SRC-047(page=4)).
- The acknowledgments and named assistance further compromise anonymity and should be removed or anonymized for double-blind review (SRC-055(page=5), SRC-056(page=5)).

Detailed assessment by sub-dimension:
- POL-ETH: strength: The work is evaluated on standard classification benchmarks and does not directly claim deployment in sensitive domains, which reduces immediate harm concerns (SRC-038(page=3)). weakness: The paper provides no discussion of fairness, bias, misuse, or limitations if few-shot classifiers are deployed in socially consequential settings, despite presenting a general method for adapting to new classes from very few examples (SRC-010(page=0), SRC-054(page=5)). evidence: SRC-010(page=0), SRC-038(page=3), SRC-054(page=5).
- POL-DAT: strength: The paper identifies benchmark datasets and cites the corresponding sources, including Omniglot, miniImageNet/ImageNet, and CUB-200 (SRC-038(page=3), SRC-040(page=4), SRC-043(page=4), SRC-047(page=4)). weakness: It does not document data-use permissions, license terms, consent, privacy considerations, or redistribution constraints for any dataset; this is especially relevant because Omniglot examples were drawn by human subjects and CUB/ImageNet are image datasets with their own usage terms (SRC-040(page=4), SRC-043(page=4), SRC-047(page=4)). evidence: SRC-040(page=4), SRC-043(page=4), SRC-047(page=4), SRC-050(page=5).
- POL-ANO: strength: None under a double-blind standard; the paper is fully identified. weakness: The title page lists author names and affiliations, including University of Toronto and Twitter, and the acknowledgments name collaborators, all of which directly reveal author identity or network if submitted to a double-blind venue (SRC-002(page=0), SRC-003(page=0), SRC-004(page=0), SRC-055(page=5), SRC-056(page=5)). evidence: SRC-002(page=0), SRC-003(page=0), SRC-004(page=0), SRC-056(page=5).
- POL-PLG: strength: The paper provides extensive citations to prior work and explicitly positions its method relative to matching networks, nearest class mean classifiers, neural statistician, and other one-shot learning methods (SRC-015(page=1), SRC-016(page=1), SRC-017(page=1), SRC-019(page=2)). weakness: I see no direct evidence of plagiarism or dual submission from the provided text, but this cannot be fully verified without external similarity checks; the method also builds closely on episodic training from Vinyals et al., though that dependency is acknowledged (SRC-016(page=1), SRC-024(page=2)). evidence: SRC-016(page=1), SRC-024(page=2).
- POL-IMP: strength: The paper’s dataset and benchmark choices are transparent at a high level, and it describes how the zero-shot CUB setup uses attributes and bounding boxes following prior procedures (SRC-047(page=4), SRC-049(page=5), SRC-050(page=5)). weakness: There is no broader-impact statement, checklist, license disclosure, compliance statement, or IRB/ethics approval note; the conclusion focuses entirely on technical performance and efficiency rather than societal implications or responsible deployment constraints (SRC-053(page=5), SRC-054(page=5)). evidence: SRC-049(page=5), SRC-050(page=5), SRC-053(page=5), SRC-054(page=5).

Evidence anchors used:
- SRC-002(page=0): Shows the paper includes author names, directly relevant to anonymity.
- SRC-003(page=0): Shows the University of Toronto affiliation, directly identifying authors.
- SRC-004(page=0): Shows the Twitter affiliation, directly identifying an author.
- SRC-010(page=0): Establishes the general-purpose few-shot classifier contribution, relevant to potential deployment and misuse considerations.
- SRC-012(page=1): Shows extension to zero-shot learning using class attributes, relevant to broader use beyond the core benchmark.
- SRC-015(page=1): Shows citation and differentiation from nearest class mean work, relevant to originality assessment.
- SRC-016(page=1): Shows acknowledgment of matching networks and episodic training, relevant to proper attribution.
- SRC-024(page=2): Shows the method adopts episodic training similar to Vinyals et al., relevant to attribution.
- SRC-038(page=3): Lists the datasets used across few-shot and zero-shot experiments, relevant to data compliance.
- SRC-040(page=4): Describes Omniglot as human-subject-drawn characters and gives split/augmentation details, relevant to consent/privacy documentation.
- SRC-043(page=4): Describes miniImageNet as derived from ImageNet, relevant to dataset licensing and permitted use.
- SRC-047(page=4): Describes CUB-200 images and split use, relevant to dataset compliance.
- SRC-049(page=5): Notes use of ground-truth bounding boxes for CUB, relevant to annotation/data-use transparency.
- SRC-050(page=5): Describes use of CUB class attributes and a pretrained AlexNet, relevant to data/model-source compliance.
- SRC-054(page=5): Shows the conclusion lacks broader-impact or compliance discussion and focuses on technical claims.
- SRC-056(page=5): Shows acknowledgments naming individuals, further compromising anonymity in double-blind review.

Key questions for the authors:
- Is this submission intended for a double-blind venue? If so, why are author names, affiliations, and acknowledgments included?
- What are the licenses and permitted-use terms for Omniglot, miniImageNet/ImageNet-derived data, CUB-200, pretrained AlexNet, and any released code?
- Do the Omniglot human-drawn characters and CUB/ImageNet-derived images require any consent, privacy, or ethics documentation for this use?
- Can the authors add a responsible-use discussion covering bias, domain shift, and risks from few-shot adaptation in sensitive classification settings?
- Will the authors include a broader-impact/checklist section and clarify whether IRB review was not required or was obtained?

Recommendation: Weak Reject
reviews.Final Meta-Reviewer:
Final summary: The paper proposes prototypical networks, a simple metric-based meta-learning approach for few-shot classification that represents each class by the mean of its support examples in a learned embedding and classifies queries via a softmax over negative squared Euclidean distances to class prototypes. The model is trained episodically to mimic few-shot evaluation. A clear analysis shows equivalence to a linear classifier with weights and biases determined by prototypes, clarifying the model’s inductive bias. The authors also extend the prototype idea to zero-shot learning by embedding class attributes as prototypes. Experiments on Omniglot and miniImageNet show competitive performance (state-of-the-art on Omniglot under the reported protocol, competitive on miniImageNet), and CUB zero-shot results are reported as state-of-the-art. The contribution is technically clean and practically attractive due to its simplicity and favorable scaling versus attention over support examples, though the paper lacks some reproducibility details, statistical reporting, and empirical runtime/memory validation. There are also policy/compliance issues to address if the venue requires double-blind review and broader-impact/ethics disclosures.

Consensus strengths:
- Simple, well-motivated method with explicit formulation: class prototypes as support-set means in embedding space and softmax over Euclidean distances; trained with episodic sampling (SRC-021(page=2), SRC-022(page=2), SRC-024(page=2)).
- Useful analytical insight: equivalence to a linear classifier with prototype-derived weights/biases, clarifying the inductive bias and contrasting with nearest-neighbor-style approaches (SRC-028(page=2), SRC-030(page=3)).
- Clear positioning relative to prior work (NCA, nearest class mean, matching networks, neural statistician), and a practical scalability advantage over attention across all support examples (SRC-015(page=1), SRC-016(page=1)).
- Empirical coverage of standard benchmarks and a natural zero-shot extension using attribute embeddings as class prototypes; strong results on Omniglot and CUB (SRC-038(page=3), SRC-041(page=4), SRC-050(page=5), SRC-051(page=5)).
- Readable presentation and logical structure; the main concepts and notation are easy to follow for expert readers.

Consensus weaknesses:
- Insufficient reproducibility details: missing optimizer, learning-rate schedules, episodes/iterations, query sizes, validation/model-selection protocol, seeds, and per-experiment specification of prototype normalization (SRC-040(page=4), SRC-044(page=4), SRC-036(page=3), SRC-050(page=5)).
- Statistical rigor is limited: results are reported as point estimates without confidence intervals, variance across runs, or significance testing, especially important where gains are small (SRC-041(page=4), SRC-044(page=4), SRC-051(page=5)).
- Scalability claims (vs. attention over all support examples) are not backed by runtime/memory experiments varying support-set size (SRC-006(page=0), SRC-016(page=1)).
- Ablations are sparse: prototype normalization is motivated but not quantitatively dissected; the single-prototype assumption is not empirically probed versus multi-prototype alternatives (SRC-036(page=3), SRC-032(page=3)).
- MiniImageNet performance is competitive but not consistently superior to contemporaneous baselines in 5-way settings; claims should be calibrated accordingly (SRC-044(page=4), SRC-045(page=4)).
- Minor notation/presentation issues (e.g., softmax denominator/prototype indexing and a transpose typo in the expansion around Equation 4) and sparse figure/table annotations (SRC-022(page=2), SRC-028(page=2), SRC-045(page=4), SRC-057(page=6)).
- Policy/compliance: the submission is not anonymized and includes acknowledgments; no broader-impact/ethics or dataset licensing/consent discussion is provided (SRC-055(page=5), SRC-056(page=5)).

Cross-review synthesis:
- QUAL: Agrees the method is technically sound and clean, with appropriate benchmarks and design analysis. Highlights missing training details, lack of statistical reporting, absence of runtime scaling validation, and the need for calibrated claims on miniImageNet. Overall positive on quality with caveats (SRC-021(page=2), SRC-022(page=2), SRC-028(page=2), SRC-044(page=4)).
- CLAR: Finds the paper well written and organized with clear notation for core elements, but requests pseudocode for episodic training/inference, fuller experimental details, minor notation fixes, and richer figure/table annotations. Clarity is strong but can be improved for reproducibility and precision (SRC-024(page=2), SRC-022(page=2), SRC-045(page=4), SRC-057(page=6)).
- SIGN: Evaluates the work as broadly significant due to its simplicity, scaling benefits, and strong Omniglot/CUB results, while noting unevenness on miniImageNet, lack of uncertainty reporting, and absence of quantified efficiency or broader-impact discussion. Overall impact is high within few-shot/zero-shot image classification (SRC-006(page=0), SRC-041(page=4), SRC-051(page=5)).
- ORIG: Judges the novelty as a principled and effective recombination (nearest-class-mean inductive bias with learned nonlinear embedding and episodic meta-training), with insightful but limited analysis and a creative zero-shot extension. Not a new problem setting; originality resides in the clean integration and empirical validation (SRC-015(page=1), SRC-024(page=2), SRC-028(page=2), SRC-050(page=5)).
- POL: Flags strong compliance issues if the venue is double-blind (paper lists authors/affiliations and acknowledgments) and the lack of ethics/broader-impact and dataset-license/consent disclosures. While the technical risk is low, these are process and transparency gaps that must be remedied (SRC-055(page=5), SRC-056(page=5)).

Evidence anchors used:
- SRC-006(page=0): Motivates simplicity and improved scaling versus attention over all support examples.
- SRC-015(page=1): Positions against nearest class mean and clarifies the non-linear embedding and few-shot episodic training distinction.
- SRC-016(page=1): Contrasts with matching networks and emphasizes scalability advantages.
- SRC-021(page=2): Defines prototype computation as the mean of embedded support examples.
- SRC-022(page=2): Defines the softmax over squared Euclidean distances for class probabilities.
- SRC-024(page=2): Specifies episodic training to mimic few-shot evaluation.
- SRC-028(page=2): Provides the linear-classifier equivalence analysis and associated derivation.
- SRC-032(page=3): Discusses the single- vs. multi-prototype trade-offs and computational considerations.
- SRC-036(page=3): States the normalization design choice and its claimed benefits.
- SRC-038(page=3): Lists the datasets used for few-shot and zero-shot experiments.
- SRC-041(page=4): Reports strong Omniglot performance relative to matching networks.
- SRC-044(page=4): Describes miniImageNet setup and training choices; indicates competitive results.
- SRC-051(page=5): Claims state-of-the-art on CUB zero-shot and end-to-end simplicity.
- SRC-055(page=5), SRC-056(page=5): Shows acknowledgments and named thanks, relevant to anonymization concerns.

Final score (1-10): 7
Final recommendation: Weak Accept

Actionable suggestions:
- Reproducibility and reporting:
  - Provide full training details: optimizer, learning-rate schedule, number of episodes/iterations, query examples per class/episode, regularization, initialization, validation/model-selection protocol, and random seeds for all experiments (Omniglot, miniImageNet, CUB).
  - Report results over multiple runs with confidence intervals or standard errors across sampled episodes and seeds; include significance tests where improvements are small.
  - Add concise pseudocode for episodic training and test-time inference (support/query sampling, prototype computation/updates, and, for zero-shot, attribute-prototype construction).
- Empirical validation and ablations:
  - Quantify the claimed computational/scaling benefits with runtime and memory comparisons versus matching networks as support set size varies.
  - Include ablations on prototype normalization (with/without) showing its effect on convergence speed and final accuracy on each benchmark.
  - Consider probing the single-prototype assumption, e.g., via a controlled multi-prototype variant or analysis of intra-class multimodality, to delineate regimes where one prototype is sufficient.
  - Calibrate miniImageNet claims and discuss the sensitivity to episode “way” at training versus 5-way evaluation.
- Presentation:
  - Fix minor notation issues (softmax denominator indexing; clean up Equation (4) transpose/typo) and clarify figure/table annotations; add error bars and detailed captions (e.g., clarify Figure 1 legends and the number of classes shown).
- Policy and ethics:
  - If the venue is double-blind, ensure proper anonymization: remove author names/affiliations and acknowledgments from the submission.
  - Add a brief broader-impact/limitations section discussing potential misuse, fairness, and domain shift considerations for few-shot classifiers.
  - Include dataset license/usage notes and clarify that IRB/ethics approval was not required (or obtained) for the use of Omniglot, ImageNet/miniImageNet, and CUB-200, noting any consent/privacy considerations, and disclose sources of pretrained models (e.g., AlexNet) and their licenses.

retrieved_papers.abstract: Machine comprehension of text is an important problem in natural language processing. A recently released dataset, the Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD), offers a large number of real questions and their answers created by humans through crowdsourcing. SQuAD provides a challenging testbed for evaluating machine comprehension algorithms, partly because compared with previous datasets, in SQuAD the answers do not come from a small set of candidate answers and they have variable lengths. We propose an end-to-end neural architecture for the task. The architecture is based on match-LSTM, a model we proposed previously for textual entailment, and Pointer Net, a sequence-to-sequence model proposed by Vinyals et al.(2015) to constrain the output tokens to be from the input sequences. We propose two ways of using Pointer Net for our task. Our experiments show that both of our two models substantially outperform the best results obtained by Rajpurkar et al.(2016) using logistic regression and manually crafted features.

ABSTRACT

Machine comprehension of text is an important problem in natural language processing. A recently released dataset, the Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD), offers a large number of real questions and their answers created by humans through crowdsourcing. SQuAD provides a challenging testbed for evaluating machine comprehension algorithms, partly because compared with previous datasets, in SQuAD the answers do not come from a small set of candidate answers and they have variable lengths.
1 INTRODUCTION

While the ability of a machine to understand text can be assessed in many different ways, in recent years, several benchmark datasets have been created to focus on answering questions as a way to evaluate machine comprehension (Richardson et al., 2013; Hermann et al., 2015; Hill et al., 2016; Weston et al., 2016; Rajpurkar et al., 2016). 2 METHOD

In this section, we first briefly review match-LSTM and Pointer Net. These two pieces of existing work lay the foundation of our method. We then present our end-to-end neural architecture for machine comprehension.
2.1 MATCH-LSTM

In a recent work on learning natural language inference, we proposed a match-LSTM model for predicting textual entailment (Wang & Jiang, 2016). In textual entailment, two sentences are given where one is a premise and the other is a hypothesis. To predict whether the premise entails the hypothesis, the match-LSTM model goes through the tokens of the hypothesis sequentially. At each position of the hypothesis, attention mechanism is used to obtain a weighted vector representation of the premise.

2.2 POINTER NET

Vinyals et al. (2015) proposed a Pointer Network (Ptr-Net) model to solve a special kind of problems where we want to generate an output sequence whose tokens must come from the input sequence. Instead of picking an output token from a fixed vocabulary, Ptr-Net uses attention mechanism as a pointer to select a position from the input sequence as an output symbol. 3 EXPERIMENTS
In this section, we present our experiment results and perform some analyses to better understand how our models work.
3.1 DATA

We use the Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD) v1.1 to conduct our experiments. Passages in SQuAD come from 536 articles from Wikipedia covering a wide range of topics. Each passage is a single paragraph from a Wikipedia article, and each passage has around 5 questions associated with it. In total, there are 23,215 passages and 107,785 questions. The data has been split into a training set (with 87,599 question-answer pairs), a development set (with 10,570 question-answer pairs) and a hi
3.2 EXPERIMENT SETTINGS

We first tokenize all the passages, questions and answers. The resulting vocabulary contains 117K unique words. We use word embeddings from GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014) to initialize the model. Words not found in GloVe are initialized as zero vectors. The word embeddings are not updated during the training of the model.

The dimensionality  $l$  of the hidden layers is set to be 150 or 300. We use ADAMAX (Kingma & Ba, 2015) with the coefficients  $\beta_{1} = 0.9$  and  $\beta_{2} = 0.999$  to optimize the model. Each update is computed through a minibatch of 30 instances. We do not use L2-regularization.

The performance is measured by two metrics: percentage of exact match with the ground truth answers, and word-level F1 score when comparing the tokens in the predicted answers with the tokens in the ground truth answers. Note that in the development set and the test set each question has around three ground truth answers. F1 scores with the best matching answers are used to compute the average F1 score.

Reviewer dimension: QUAL
Paper summary: The paper proposes an end-to-end neural architecture for extractive machine comprehension on SQuAD v1.1. It builds on match-LSTM to align passage tokens to the question via attention in both directions, and employs a Pointer Network-based Answer Pointer layer in two variants: a sequence model that points to a sequence of passage positions (with a learned stop token), and a boundary model that predicts start and end indices of the answer span. An additional search mechanism constrains span length at inference. Experiments on SQuAD show clear gains over the logistic regression baseline, with the boundary model outperforming the sequence model. The authors provide analyses by answer length, question type, and attention visualizations.

Strengths:
- Clear and technically consistent formulation of match-LSTM with attention in both directions and integration with Pointer Networks for both sequence and boundary formulations. Equations and architectural components are well specified. 
- Experimental setup on SQuAD is appropriate with standard metrics (Exact Match and F1), and results demonstrate substantial improvements over a strong feature-engineered baseline. 
- The boundary model design choice is well motivated for extractive QA and empirically superior to the sequence model; the added span-length-constrained search is a pragmatic improvement.
- Useful qualitative and quantitative analyses (by answer length and question type) and attention visualizations that diagnose model behavior.

Weaknesses:
- Limited statistical rigor: no reporting of variance, multiple runs, or significance tests; conclusions rely on point estimates.
- Reproducibility details are incomplete: several training specifics (e.g., learning rates, training duration/epochs, gradient clipping, early stopping) and code availability are not provided.
- Comparisons to prior work are narrow: baselines include the original SQuAD logistic regression and one additional reference, with no broader evaluation against contemporaneous neural baselines in detail within the paper body.
- The boundary model’s inference uses a heuristic independence p(a_s) × p(a_e) and a hard span-length constraint without ablation or justification of its sensitivity.

reviews.Reviewer SIGN:
Reviewer dimension: SIGN
Paper summary: The paper proposes an end-to-end neural architecture for extractive machine comprehension on SQuAD v1.1 that combines a match-LSTM attention mechanism with a Pointer Network. Two variants are introduced: a sequence model that predicts a sequence of answer token positions and a boundary model that predicts start and end indices of a contiguous span. A search mechanism further refines span selection by constraining length. Experiments on SQuAD show both models outperform a feature-engineered logistic regression baseline, with the boundary model achieving 61.1% exact match and 71.2% F1 on the development set, and further improvements with search and bidirectional preprocessing (Table 2; text references).

Dimension score (1-10): 8
Confidence (1-5): 4

Sub-dimension scores:
- SIGN-BRD: 8/10
- SIGN-DOM: 9/10
- SIGN-SOT: 7/10
- SIGN-IMP: 3/10

Strengths:
- Tackles a broadly important problem—moving machine reading comprehension beyond candidate selection to variable-length span prediction—with a general, end-to-end neural approach likely to influence subsequent QA research paradigms (SRC-036(page=2), SRC-037(page=2), SRC-039(page=3)).
- Provides two principled formulations (sequence vs. boundary) grounded in a pointer mechanism, addressing the consecutivity constraint central to modern extractive QA (SRC-036(page=2), SRC-037(page=2), SRC-038(page=3)).
- Demonstrates clear and substantial gains over strong feature-based baselines on SQuAD, a widely adopted benchmark, and offers analyses that deepen understanding of when the model succeeds or fails (e.g., by answer length and question type) (SRC-072(page=5), SRC-074(page=6), SRC-077(page=6), SRC-078(page=7)).
- Introduces a practical span search refinement that improves boundary predictions, emphasizing applicability to real extractive QA inference (SRC-062(page=5)).

Weaknesses:
- While competitive, improvements toward the top state-of-the-art are not comprehensively quantified against the strongest contemporary neural baselines within the paper’s tables; most emphasis is on surpassing logistic regression, leaving the magnitude of gains versus recent neural systems less explicit (SRC-072(page=5), SRC-074(page=6)).
- The paper does not discuss real-world or societal implications (e.g., fairness, bias in Wikipedia-derived QA, or environmental cost), missing an opportunity to contextualize potential broader impacts or risks. The sectioning and content focus on methods, experiments, and related work, with no impact discussion (SRC-063(page=5), SRC-080(page=7)).
- Domain generality beyond SQuAD is not empirically established; it remains unclear how the approach would transfer to other domains or datasets with different answer distributions without candidate spans (SRC-066(page=5)).

Detailed assessment by sub-dimension:
- SIGN-BRD: strength: The work addresses a significant methodological gap for machine comprehension—predicting variable-length, contiguous spans directly from passages—and proposes a general pointer-based paradigm that can be adapted across sequence labeling/extraction tasks. By integrating match-LSTM attention with a pointer mechanism and formulating both sequence and boundary variants, it provides a broadly influential modeling blueprint (SRC-036(page=2), SRC-037(page=2), SRC-039(page=3)). weakness: The paper’s empirical focus is limited to a single dataset (SQuAD), constraining demonstrated breadth of influence across tasks or modalities (SRC-066(page=5)). evidence: SRC-036(page=2); SRC-037(page=2); SRC-039(page=3); SRC-066(page=5).
- SIGN-DOM: strength: Within NLP QA, the method clearly outperforms feature-based baselines on SQuAD and offers actionable refinements (search over span lengths) that yield tangible gains. The boundary formulation shows stronger exact match and F1 than the sequence variant, indicating a practical, domain-appropriate design choice for extractive QA (SRC-062(page=5), SRC-072(page=5), SRC-074(page=6)). weakness: Domain benefits are shown only for SQuAD, without evaluation on other QA benchmarks (e.g., cloze-style or multi-document), limiting claims of domain-wide superiority (SRC-066(page=5)). evidence: SRC-062(page=5); SRC-072(page=5); SRC-074(page=6); SRC-066(page=5).
- SIGN-SOT: strength: The paper reports substantial, consistent improvements over a strong, carefully engineered logistic regression baseline from Rajpurkar et al., with the boundary model achieving 61.1% EM and 71.2% F1 on development data, and additional gains from search and bidirectional preprocessing (SRC-072(page=5), SRC-074(page=6), SRC-061(page=5)). weakness: The comparison set does not fully cover the strongest contemporary neural baselines in-table; thus, while improvements are meaningful, the absolute advance over the state-of-the-art is not conclusively demonstrated within the paper’s reported comparisons (SRC-072(page=5), SRC-074(page=6)). evidence: SRC-061(page=5); SRC-072(page=5); SRC-074(page=6).
- SIGN-IMP: strength: SQuAD is a high-visibility benchmark with practical relevance to applications such as question answering over knowledge sources; the model’s end-to-end nature and span prediction mechanism are practically useful for building QA systems (SRC-066(page=5), SRC-070(page=5)). weakness: The paper lacks a discussion of societal impact, including fairness, bias, or environmental considerations, and does not articulate who benefits or may be harmed by deployment. No ethics or impact section is present among the described sections (methods, experiments, related work) (SRC-063(page=5), SRC-080(page=7)). evidence: SRC-066(page=5); SRC-070(page=5); SRC-063(page=5); SRC-080(page=7).

Evidence anchors used:
- SRC-036(page=2): Introduces the sequence-pointer formulation for selecting answer token positions from the passage; supports significance of handling variable-length answers.
- SRC-037(page=2): Introduces the boundary-pointer formulation ensuring consecutivity; central to extractive QA span prediction significance.
- SRC-039(page=3): Describes the three-layer architecture (preprocessing LSTM, match-LSTM, Answer Pointer), evidencing a general end-to-end design.
- SRC-062(page=5): Describes the span search refinement and combining bidirectional Ans-Ptr, evidencing practical enhancements.
- SRC-066(page=5): Details SQuAD’s scope and composition, underscoring domain relevance.
- SRC-070(page=5): Defines evaluation metrics (EM and F1), grounding performance interpretation.
- SRC-072(page=5): States that the proposed models outperform baselines; supports significance in-domain.
- SRC-074(page=6): Reports quantitative gains of the boundary model over the sequence model (61.1% EM, 71.2% F1) and over logistic regression; supports SOTA improvement assessment.
- SRC-063(page=5), SRC-080(page=7): Show the paper’s focus on experiments and related work with no dedicated societal impact discussion.

Key questions for the authors:
- Can you provide a more comprehensive comparison against the strongest concurrent neural baselines to clarify the margin to state-of-the-art and the robustness of gains across settings?
- How does the method generalize to other QA datasets (e.g., different domains or answer distributions)? Any evidence beyond SQuAD or discussion of transfer?
- What are the computational costs (training/inference time, parameter counts), and how do they compare to the baselines?
- Could you discuss potential societal impacts (e.g., biases in Wikipedia-derived data, fairness in downstream QA applications, and environmental cost of training), and any mitigations?

Recommendation: Weak Accept

Paper summary: The paper targets extractive machine comprehension on SQuAD, proposing end-to-end neural models that combine match-LSTM (adapted from the authors’ prior textual entailment work) with Pointer Networks to predict answers as spans from the passage. Two Answer Pointer formulations are introduced: a sequence model that selects a series of positions (not enforcing contiguity) and a boundary model that predicts start and end indices to enforce contiguity, with an additional span-length–limited search during inference. Empirical results on SQuAD show substantial improvements over a feature-engineered baseline, and analyses include attention visualizations and breakdowns by answer length and question type.

reviews.Final Meta-Reviewer:
Final summary: This paper proposes an end-to-end neural architecture for extractive machine comprehension on SQuAD, combining a question-aware passage encoder (match-LSTM) with a Pointer Network–based Answer Pointer in two variants: (i) a sequence model that predicts a sequence of passage positions with a learned stop symbol and (ii) a boundary model that predicts start and end indices to enforce contiguity. A simple span-length–constrained search at inference further refines predictions. On SQuAD v1.1, both variants substantially outperform a feature-engineered logistic regression baseline, with the boundary model clearly superior to the sequence model. The method is technically sound and well motivated for span extraction, but the paper’s evaluation is narrow, several training and reproducibility details are missing, the boundary model’s inference uses heuristic assumptions without ablations, and there is no discussion of ethical or broader impact considerations.

Consensus strengths:
- Clearly specified, coherent architecture that adapts match-LSTM and Ptr-Net to span extraction, with both sequence and boundary formulations articulated and justified.
- Strong empirical gains over the SQuAD logistic regression baseline, with the boundary model achieving higher EM/F1 than the sequence model.
- Practical inference refinement via a span-length–constrained search; reasonable analyses by answer length, question type, and attention visualizations that illuminate behavior.
- Appropriate experimental setup and standard evaluation metrics on a widely used benchmark.

Consensus weaknesses:
- Limited comparative evaluation against contemporaneous neural baselines; emphasis is largely on surpassing a feature-based baseline, leaving gaps about margins to the strongest systems.
- Reproducibility gaps: missing learning rate/schedule, epochs/early stopping, gradient clipping, regularization (e.g., dropout), random seeds, and code availability; no variance or significance testing.
- Heuristic independence assumption p(a_s) × p(a_e) and hard span length cap in the boundary search are not justified or ablated; lack of joint modeling of start–end may mis-rank spans, especially for longer answers.
- Presentation issues: minor typographical inconsistencies (e.g., “Prr-Net”), incomplete/missing definitions (e_Q and some equations), and limited procedural detail for the Answer Pointer.
- No ethics/broader impact or data licensing discussion; potential biases in Wikipedia/crowdsourced data are unaddressed.

Cross-review synthesis:
- QUAL: Finds the method sound and well specified, with solid results and insightful analyses, but notes limited baselines, lack of statistical rigor, and heuristic boundary search without ablation. Reproducibility details are insufficient.
- CLAR: Overall clear structure and figures, but some typos, incomplete notation/definitions, and a lack of step-by-step specification for the Answer Pointer reduce clarity. Figure captions and axis labeling could be improved.
- SIGN: Deems the contribution significant within QA for moving to contiguous span prediction with a general pointer-based paradigm and showing clear gains on SQuAD. However, breadth beyond SQuAD and comparison to the strongest neural baselines are limited; no discussion of societal impact.
- ORIG: Novelty stems from a coherent combination and task-aware instantiations (sequence vs. boundary) rather than fundamentally new primitives; the search heuristic is a simple but effective addition. No new problem/benchmark is introduced.
- POL: Raises concerns about missing discussion of ethical risks, dataset biases, licenses/consent for crowdsourced data, and broader impacts; otherwise proper citation practice is observed.

Evidence anchors used:
- SRC-054(page=4), SRC-055(page=4), SRC-056(page=4): Define the sequence Answer Pointer with attention over P+1 positions and a stop symbol; supports the sequence formulation and stopping mechanism.
- SRC-060(page=4): Defines the boundary model predicting start and end indices; central to enforcing contiguity.
- SRC-062(page=5): Describes the span-length–limited search and independence assumption p(a_s) × p(a_e); highlights heuristic inference choices.
- SRC-066(page=5): Provides SQuAD dataset details; supports the experimental setting and scope.
- SRC-068(page=5), SRC-069(page=5): States embeddings, optimizer, hidden sizes, and batch size; underscores missing training specifics (e.g., learning rate, epochs).
- SRC-070(page=5): Specifies evaluation metrics (EM and F1); grounds performance assessment.
- SRC-072(page=5); SRC-074(page=6) (pages=5–6): Report that both models outperform the logistic regression baseline and quantify boundary model performance (61.1% EM, 71.2% F1); supports claimed improvements and relative ranking of variants.
- SRC-061(page=5): Notes “Search,” bidirectional preprocessing (“b”), and ensemble (“en”) in Table 2; indicates ablation factors mentioned but not fully elaborated.
- SRC-045(page=3); SRC-048(page=3): Reveal notational gaps (e_Q replication operator) and incomplete post-equation text; supports clarity concerns.
- SRC-077(page=6), SRC-078(page=7), SRC-079(page=7); SRC-073(page=6) (pages=6–7): Provide analyses by answer length and question type and attention visualizations; support interpretability and identified failure modes.

Final score (1-10): 6
Final recommendation: Weak Accept

Actionable suggestions:
- Expand the comparative evaluation to include more concurrent neural baselines and report margins to then–state-of-the-art systems in the main results table; include parameter counts and compute costs for context.
- Provide full training and evaluation details (learning rate and schedule, number of epochs, early stopping, gradient clipping, regularization such as dropout, random seeds) and, if possible, average results over multiple runs with standard deviations or confidence intervals; release code and preprocessing scripts.
- Justify and ablate the boundary model’s inference choices: evaluate sensitivity to the span length cap and the independence assumption; consider a joint start–end decoder (e.g., conditioned end on start) to capture dependence and reduce mis-ranking.
- Clarify the Answer Pointer procedure with a concise, self-contained algorithm/pseudocode for both variants, including inputs/outputs, β_k computation, stopping, and the exact loss factorization.
- Clean up notation and presentation: define e_Q and the ⊗ operator explicitly at first use; correct typographical issues (“Ptr-Net” consistently); enrich figure captions with axis labels and dimensional annotations.
- Add an ethics/broader impact discussion: acknowledge potential biases in Wikipedia/crowdsourced data, discuss implications for downstream QA systems, data and embedding licenses (SQuAD, GloVe), and outline mitigation strategies for bias and responsible deployment.

retrieved_papers.title: CausalGAN: Learning Causal Implicit Generative Models with Adversarial Training

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.02023, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

retrieved_papers.abstract: We propose an adversarial training procedure for learning a causal implicit generative model for a given causal graph. We show that adversarial training can be used to learn a generative model with true observational and interventional distributions if the generator architecture is consistent with the given causal graph. We consider the application of generating faces based on given binary labels where the dependency structure between the labels is preserved with a causal graph. This problem can be seen as learning a causal implicit generative model for the image and labels. We devise a two-stage procedure for this problem. First we train a causal implicit generative model over binary labels using a neural network consistent with a causal graph as the generator. We empirically show that WassersteinGAN can be used to output discrete labels. Later, we propose two new conditional GAN architectures, which we call CausalGAN and CausalBEGAN. We show that the optimal generator of the CausalGAN, given the labels, samples from the image distributions conditioned on these labels. The conditional GAN combined with a trained causal implicit generative model for the labels is then a causal implicit generative model over the labels and the generated image. We show that the proposed architectures can be used to sample from observational and interventional image distributions, even for interventions which do not naturally occur in the dataset.

retrieved_papers.title: Learning Implicit Generative Models by Matching Perceptual Features

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.02762, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

retrieved_papers.abstract: Perceptual features (PFs) have been used with great success in tasks such as transfer learning, style transfer, and super-resolution. However, the efficacy of PFs as key source of information for learning generative models is not well studied. We investigate here the use of PFs in the context of learning implicit generative models through moment matching (MM). More specifically, we propose a new effective MM approach that learns implicit generative models by performing mean and covariance matching of features extracted from pretrained ConvNets. Our proposed approach improves upon existing MM methods by: (1) breaking away from the problematic min/max game of adversarial learning; (2) avoiding online learning of kernel functions; and (3) being efficient with respect to both number of used moments and required minibatch size. Our experimental results demonstrate that, due to the expressiveness of PFs from pretrained deep ConvNets, our method achieves state-of-the-art results for challenging benchmarks.

retrieved_papers.title: Robust training of implicit generative models for multivariate and heavy-tailed distributions with an invariant statistical loss

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.22381, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

retrieved_papers.abstract: Traditional implicit generative models are capable of learning highly complex data distributions. However, their training involves distinguishing real data from synthetically generated data using adversarial discriminators, which can lead to unstable training dynamics and mode dropping issues. In this work, we build on the \textit{invariant statistical loss} (ISL) method introduced in \cite{de2024training}, and extend it to handle heavy-tailed and multivariate data distributions. The data generated by many real-world phenomena can only be properly characterised using heavy-tailed probability distributions, and traditional implicit methods struggle to effectively capture their asymptotic behavior. To address this problem, we introduce a generator trained with ISL, that uses input noise from a generalised Pareto distribution (GPD). We refer to this generative scheme as Pareto-ISL for conciseness. Our experiments demonstrate that Pareto-ISL accurately models the tails of the distributions while still effectively capturing their central characteristics. The original ISL function was conceived for 1D data sets. When the actual data is $n$-dimensional, a straightforward extension of the method was obtained by targeting the $n$ marginal distributions of the data. This approach is computationally infeasible and ineffective in high-dimensional spaces. To overcome this, we extend the 1D approach using random projections and define a new loss function suited for multivariate data, keeping problems tractable by adjusting the number of projections. We assess its performance in multidimensional generative modeling and explore its potential as a pretraining technique for generative adversarial networks (GANs) to prevent mode collapse, reporting promising results and highlighting its robustness across various hyperparameter settings.

retrieved_papers.title: Learning Implicit Generative Models with Theoretical Guarantees

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.02862, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

retrieved_papers.abstract: We propose a \textbf{uni}fied \textbf{f}ramework for \textbf{i}mplicit \textbf{ge}nerative \textbf{m}odeling (UnifiGem) with theoretical guarantees by integrating approaches from optimal transport, numerical ODE, density-ratio (density-difference) estimation and deep neural networks. First, the problem of implicit generative learning is formulated as that of finding the optimal transport map between the reference distribution and the target distribution, which is characterized by a totally nonlinear Monge-Ampere equation. Interpreting the infinitesimal linearization of the Monge-Ampere equation from the perspective of gradient flows in measure spaces leads to the continuity equation or the McKean-Vlasov equation. We then solve the McKean-Vlasov equation numerically using the forward Euler iteration, where the forward Euler map depends on the density ratio (density difference) between the distribution at current iteration and the underlying target distribution. We further estimate the density ratio (density difference) via deep density-ratio (density-difference) fitting and derive explicit upper bounds on the estimation error. Experimental results on both synthetic datasets and real benchmark datasets support our theoretical findings and demonstrate the effectiveness of UnifiGem.

retrieved_papers.title: Learning the Base Distribution in Implicit Generative Models

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.04357, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

retrieved_papers.abstract: Popular generative model learning methods such as Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), and Variational Autoencoders (VAE) enforce the latent representation to follow simple distributions such as isotropic Gaussian. In this paper, we argue that learning a complicated distribution over the latent space of an auto-encoder enables more accurate modeling of complicated data distributions. Based on this observation, we propose a two stage optimization procedure which maximizes an approximate implicit density model. We experimentally verify that our method outperforms GANs and VAEs on two image datasets (MNIST, CELEB-A). We also show that our approach is amenable to learning generative model for sequential data, by learning to generate speech and music.

retrieved_papers.title: Learning Implicit Generative Models by Teaching Explicit Ones

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.03870, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

retrieved_papers.abstract: Implicit generative models are difficult to train as no explicit density functions are defined. Generative adversarial nets (GANs) present a minimax framework to train such models, which however can suffer from mode collapse due to the nature of the JS-divergence. This paper presents a learning by teaching (LBT) approach to learning implicit models, which intrinsically avoids the mode collapse problem by optimizing a KL-divergence rather than the JS-divergence in GANs. In LBT, an auxiliary explicit model is introduced to fit the distribution defined by the implicit model while the later one teaches the explicit model to match the data distribution. LBT is formulated as a bilevel optimization problem, whose optimal generator matches the true data distribution. LBT can be naturally integrated with GANs to derive a hybrid LBT-GAN that enjoys complimentary benefits. %implies that we obtain the maximum likelihood estimation of the implicit model. Finally, we present a stochastic gradient ascent algorithm with unrolling to solve the challenging learning problems. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

source_anchors.text: LEARNING IN IMPLICIT GENERATIVE MODELS
Shakir Mohamed and Balaji Lakshminarayanan
DeepMind, London
{shakir,balajiln}@google.com
ABSTRACT

Generative adversarial networks (GANs) provide an algorithmic framework for constructing generative models with several appealing properties: they do not require a likelihood function to be specified, only a generating procedure; they provide samples that are sharp and compelling; and they allow us to harness our knowledge of building highly accurate neural network classifiers. Here, we develop our understanding of GANs with the aim of forming a rich view of this growing area of machine learning
1 IMPLICIT GENERATIVE MODELS

It is useful to make a distinction between two types of probabilistic models: prescribed and implicit models (Diggle and Gratton, 1984). Prescribed probabilistic models are those that provide an explicit parametric specification of the distribution of an observed random variable  $\mathbf{x}$ , specifying a log-likelihood function  $\log q_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$  with parameters  $\theta$ . Most models in machine learning and statistics are of this form, whether they be state-of-the-art classifie

Implicit generative models use a latent variable  $\mathbf{z}$  and transform it using a deterministic function  $\mathcal{G}_{\theta}$  that maps from  $\mathbb{R}^m\to \mathbb{R}^d$  using parameters  $\pmb{\theta}$ . Such models are amongst the most fundamental of models, e.g., many of the basic methods for generating non-uniform random variates are based on simple implicit models and one-line transformations (Devroye, 2006). In general, implicit generative models specify a valid density on t

where  $q(\mathbf{z})$  is a latent variable that provides the external source of randomness and equation (2) is the definition of the transformed density as the derivative of the cumulative distribution function. When the function  $\mathcal{G}$  is well-defined, such as when the function is invertible, or has dimensions  $m = d$  with easily characterised roots, we recover the familiar rule for transformations of probability distributions.

We are interested in developing more general and flexible implicit generative models where the function  $\mathcal{G}$  is a non-linear function with  $d > m$ , specified by deep networks.
